key_insight: A compressible finite-chord scattering model can predict leading-edge noise reduction from perforated and porous inserts without fitting to acoustic data by using physically derived admittance models.
engineering_relevance: This gives aeroacoustic designers a more trustworthy way to evaluate leading-edge treatments for low-speed aircraft and wind-turbine blades, especially when the chord is not acoustically compact.
method: Solved finite-chord leading-edge scattering in compressible subsonic flow with arbitrary chordwise admittance, including wake shedding, Kutta condition, and permeability-dependent edge singularities.
Derived perforated-insert admittance from Rayleigh conductivity plus thickness, aperture-interaction, and grazing-flow blockage corrections.
Represented porous inserts using measured permeability and pore-fluid inertia, with finite-span and array-aperture effects included in the far field.
evidence_signal: Across 84 comparisons, perforated-insert predictions matched measurements to 2.5 dB rms versus 4.4 dB using unscaled impedance, and two of three porous inserts were predicted within 1.7 dB rms.
watch_item: The model does not reproduce narrow equally spaced spectral peaks seen on perforated plates, suggesting an additional convecting source not captured by the frozen-gust assumption.
paper_title: Leading-edge noise reduction by perforated and porous inserts: a compressible finite-chord prediction without fitted constants
